meta.jhaNotes:
HAZARDS	SPECIFIC PRECAUTIONS/REQUIREMENTS
	Ergonomics: Ergonomically arrange your workstation to reduce stress and eliminate potential injuries and disorders from overuse of muscles, poor posture, and repetitive motion.  Repetitive tasks such as typing may create problems for some individuals.  To avoid such problems, alternate tasks to prevent the over-exertion of a particular body part or series of parts.  Your supervisor should provide you with the latitude to alternate tasks without hindering mission effectiveness.  Schedule your daily tasks with this in mind.
	Material Handling:	Ergonomically arrange your workstation to reduce stress and eliminate potential injuries and disorders from overuse of muscles, poor posture, and repetitive motion.  Repetitive tasks such as typing may create problems for some individuals.  To avoid such problems, alternate tasks to prevent the over-exertion of a particular body part or series of parts.  Your supervisor should provide you with the latitude to alternate tasks without hindering mission effectiveness.  Schedule your daily tasks with this in mind.

You may occasionally need to lift materials manually. Strains, sprains, hernias, fractures, bruises, and lacerations may result from poor manual material handling and lifting practices. Always lift with your legs, keep the load close to your body, and do not twist while supporting the load. Wear gloves when handling sharp objects or wood materials that can splinter. If the materials are bulky or heavy (over 25 lbs) you may need to get a helper or use a dolly. Always ask for help instead of trying to do it alone.
	
	Walking/Working Surfaces:	Walk, don’t run.  Be aware of items (cords, loose carpet, pencils, paper, etc.) that may cause you to slip/trip and fall.  Climb stairs facing forward, stay to the right side, use the handrail and avoid distractions that may cause you to fall.  Do not run up or downstairs.
	
	Housekeeping: 	Take the trash out frequently and make housekeeping a priority. Clean up spills immediately. 
	
	Electrical Hazards: All of the 194th / 248th CEF staff offices use computers and other electrically powered equipment.  Ensure all electrically operated equipment has a ground prong if manufactured with one, and that all prongs are securely attached.  When plugging and unplugging electrical equipment, grasp the base of the cord.  Frequently inspect cords for damage.  If you feel a shock or tingling sensation when touching a piece of equipment, turn it off at the power strip or circuit breaker and notify your supervisor.  Multiple plug adapters will not be used solely as wiring to provide additional or more convenient outlets. Power strips should only support low-wattage equipment. Extension cords must only be used when there is no other option. Relocate the equipment if possible. If extension cords are used, do
not create tripping hazards with them. All heat-producing appliances must be plugged into a dedicated wall outlet. Contact Civil Engineering to verify that the circuit will not be overloaded.

	Fire Safety: 	All of the 194th / 248th CEF staff offices use computers and other electrically powered equipment.  Ensure all electrically operated equipment has a ground prong if manufactured with one, and that all prongs are securely attached.  When plugging and unplugging electrical equipment, grasp the base of the cord.  Frequently inspect cords for damage.  If you feel a shock or tingling sensation when touching a piece of equipment, turn it off at the power strip or circuit breaker and notify your supervisor.  Multiple plug adapters will not be used solely as wiring to provide additional or more convenient outlets. Power strips should only support low-wattage equipment. Extension cords must only be used when there is no other option. Relocate the equipment if possible. If extension cords are used, do
not create tripping hazards with them. All heat-producing appliances must be plugged into a dedicated wall outlet. Contact Civil Engineering to verify that the circuit will not be overloaded.

Never block access to electrical panels or paths of egress. Fire extinguishers, if required, must always be serviceable and ready to use. Fire extinguishers and electrical panels must have an area of 36 inches clear around them at all times.  

	Hand Tool Safety:	You may occasionally be required to use tools in the office (utility knives, screwdrivers, etc.).  Ensure you always cut away from your body.  Do not carry and/or store unguarded blades or sharp objects in your pockets or desk drawers.  There are assortments of hand tools that may be used in an office environment.  Ensure that all tools are used for the purposes for which they were designed.  Inspect tools before use.  If an unsafe tool is found, remove it from service and report it to your supervisor.

	Ladder Safety 
Personnel who use ladders at any working height shall be trained in the care and use of different types of ladders. The supervisor or a designated trainer shall conduct this training when an employee is first assigned. Refer to DAFMAN 91-203 paragraph 7.3.5 for additional information on ladder training. All training shall include hands-on instruction to include inspection of ladders for defects, possible electrocution hazards, proper positioning, and placement of ladders for various job sites.  Additional Ladder Safety Training is available at the American Ladder Safety Institute (laddersafetytraining.org). Select “Single and Extension Ladder Safety”	

	Office Safety:
Desks, tables, and many other pieces of office furniture have sharp corners that can cause injury.  Use caution, particularly when walking around desks.  Open file cabinet drawers one at a time to prevent possible tipping.  Close cabinet doors and drawers when not being used. Position office equipment in a manner that egress and ease of movement are not hampered.  Proper sitting is important, employees leaning back or sitting on the front edge of the seat creates mishaps/falls from chairs.

	Jewelry
Jewelry, such as rings, watches, bracelets, and necklaces, that presents a potential for catching, snagging, pulling, or tearing will be restricted from wear if it presents a hazard to the employee of operations, such as engaged in work in industrial areas, performing maintenance on aircraft, vehicles, equipment or machinery. Climbing, ascending, or descending activities where personnel could fall or jump from elevated surfaces. Materials handling operations. Any type of work where personnel is exposed to moving machinery, rotating or revolving parts, or activities that could result in their hands being caught by a moving part and injured. Performing work or inspection on or near energized electrical parts. Performing work on or around high-temperature equipment.  Eyewear such as metal eyeglasses shall be secured by a band or cord to prevent them from falling into energized electrical circuits or moving industrial machinery. Medic-Alert identification for medical issues is permitted to don non-dangling/non-hazardous medical alert items, e.g., clasps, medical cards in hard hats, identification badge holders, etc., to warn co-workers of potential medical issues. These restrictions do not apply to administrative and support personnel assigned office duties or visiting these areas, but not performing industrial work.

meta.medicalFacility:
There is not an emergency medical treatment facility located on Camp Murray.  The nearest Emergency medical facility is located on JBLM at the Madigan Army Medical Center.  If emergency responders are needed, call 911 from any base telephone. (Note: If you dial 911 from your cell phone, it may delay response since the call goes to an off-base responder). The Fire Department will respond with paramedics/EMTs that are on shift. They can evaluate the injuries and recommend further medical attention. If further medical attention is needed, an ambulance may be called to transport the individual to a medical facility. If it is not a severe injury, but the person feels that a doctor needs to check it, they may go to an off-base medical provider of their choice within a reasonable distance (25 miles).

meta.evacuationRoute:
Evacuation Procedures: Upon notification, evacuate the area/building immediately. Secure sensitive information (bring it with you if needed).  Do not lock doors, use the telephone, or operate any electronic equipment until you have arrived at the office assembly area.
•	The senior ranking person on duty for each workcenter is responsible for the accountability of all their personnel.  The senior ranking member at the evacuation point will ensure all personnel have been accounted.

Primary Rally Point: Parking lot along 41st Division Way/Field Artillery Trail

Alternate Rally Point: Parking lot across from B120/B126 on 41st Division Way
meta.shelterInPlace:
ON-SITE SHELTER LOCATION: If you hear, “Lockdown, Lockdown, Lockdown”, Unit personnel need to hide in their designated shelter location if they cannot evacuate. Use the following to determine a safe location and replace the information below with your designated shelter location:
a. Avoid areas with large or external windows.
b. Attempt to find a place with solid doors (no windows) and walls.
c. Avoid high traffic areas or rooms that cannot be locked or barricaded.

Building 120 Shelter Locations: Emergency Management Office

Builiding 127 Shelter Locations: Break Room

OFF-SITE SHELTER: Unit personnel will go to the PCRC Building 80 if necessary.
meta.activeShooterMethods:
RUN, HIDE, FIGHT: After being notified of an active shooter (AtHoc, GIANT VOICE, radio network, telephone, gunfire, etc), unit members should do one of the following if practicable:
a.  Run: If an active shooter is in your immediate area, attempt to evacuate if you can do so safely. Do not take any belongings. Help others if possible, but do not stop to render aid or evacuate wounded personnel. Attempt to reach an off-site shelter location. Attempt to call first responders and provide as much information as possible.
b.  Hide: If not immediately threatened, or if the active shooter is in an unknown location, or if you are unable to evacuate, make every attempt to hide your location. Lock/barricade doors, turn off lights and computers, silence cell phones/radios, and remain quiet. Do not report your location or who is with you via social media.
c. Fight: If no other options are available to you and your health and safety are under immediate threat, act aggressively and with maximum violence to disable the active shooter.
meta.fireEquipmentNotes:
Employees are required to be trained in the use of the extinguishers using the pull, aim, squeeze and sweep method (PASS). 
	(P) Pull the pin to allow you to discharge the extinguisher, 
	(A) aim at the base of the fire, 
	(S) squeeze the handle and, 
	(S) Sweep from side to side until the fire is completely out. 
	If you must evacuate the facility, get out of the building from any exit and proceed to your pre-determined meeting location as identified on the facility emergency action plan drawings. This education must be provided when a new employee is first hired, and annually thereafter.  Document on AF Form 55 link to Training can be found here: https://ehs.washington.edu/training/fire-extinguisher-training-online

meta.trafficSafetyNotes:
Mandatory use of seat belts:  Mishap experience has proven time after time that safety belts prevent injuries and save lives.  If you are involved in a vehicle mishap and you are not wearing your seatbelt, you stand a five times greater chance of being thrown from the vehicle.  Additionally, your body acts as a projectile and could strike other passengers causing death and serious injury.   Also, as a vehicle operator, you are responsible for ensuring all passengers are using safety belts.  Traffic violations for passengers not wearing safety belts go to the operator.
Note:  Placing the shoulder strap under the arm or not using/disconnecting automatic belts constitutes improper use and may result in a citation or more seriously, death or disability.
IAW DODI 6055.4 (Traffic Safety Program) and AFI 91-207, The US Air Force Traffic Safety Program, the use of headphones, earphones, and cellular telephones is prohibited while operating a vehicle on a DoD installation.  The only caveat to this is using a hands-free device or in hands-free operating mode.  
AFI 91-207, The US Air Force Traffic Safety Program, outlines the requirements for seat belt use.  Safety belts will be worn by anyone driving or riding in a vehicle on base.  Active-duty personnel must wear safety belts when operating a vehicle (regardless of whether it is a GOV or POV) on or off base.  AF civilian personnel on duty must wear seat belts on or off a DoD installation, children 1.50 meters (4 ft, 9 inches) in height or smaller regardless of age must be in an infant seat or child restraint device.
Speed limits:
•	You, as a driver must follow all speed limits on and off base.
•	On base, the general speed limit is 25 mph if no other sign is posted.
•	The basic speed limit off base is 35 mph in built-up areas and 55 mph on roadways.  Typically, on highways, it is 60 mph.  If you are hauling a trailer, camper, or boat, reduce your speed to prevent from tipping over or jackknifing.
Local traffic hazards:
•	Driving during winter in this area is extremely dangerous with ice and snow because the roads are overpopulated and there are numerous curves and hills.  Black ice can increase the risk of accidents, so slow down and take your time during the winter months.  We would rather have you arrive a few minutes late, than not at all!
•	Highway I-5:  You may or may not have heard of the motor vehicle mishaps on the I-5; however, according to the Air Force Safety Center, the Air Force loses roughly on average 18 Airmen annually due to fatal motor vehicle mishaps.  Protect yourself by reducing your speed and driving defensively.  This means expect other drivers to speed and pass at the worst times, and adjust your driving to avoid an accident.
•	Rural Roads:  Here in Washington, we have roadways 7, 8, 12, 101, 121, 161, 162, 167, 410, 507, 510, 512, and 706.  These roadways on average have a maximum speed limit of 35 mph to 60 mph.  These roadways can also become congested with traffic and occasional farm equipment.  If you are stuck behind a piece of farm equipment, do not try passing unless it is safe and legal to do so.  Be sure to plan so you do not need to rush.  Lastly, during the wintertime, these roads are secondary when it comes to sanding and plowing.  It is important to know this in case you need to make other arrangements when it comes to getting to your destination.  The most serious accidents occur when people drive faster than the road conditions will safely allow.  Use common sense and reduce your speed for poor weather conditions and congested traffic.
•	Electronic Devices: In Washington State it is illegal for a driver to hold an electronic device even when stopped at an intersection or in traffic.  Fines start at $136 for the first offense and $234 for the second, and will be reported to the driver’s insurance company and will appear on the driver’s record.
Motorcycle riders: 
Motorcycle riders must have a motorcycle endorsement from a state, and have attended a Motorcycle Safety Foundation (Basic Rider or Basic rider II Course).  Additionally, each rider must make contact with their unit Motorcycle Safety Representative (MSR).  The rider must receive a unit safety briefing from their MSR or designated representative before riding.  All riders must also complete an MSF-approved intermediate training course (sportbike riders must take a sportbike riding course) ideally within 60 days but no later than one year after completing initial training. See AFI 91-207.  Annual pre-season briefings are also required.
•	AF civilian personnel only require training if they are required to operate a motorcycle ON-DUTY.

selectedModules.title: Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)
selectedModules.reference: DAFMAN 91-203 - Air Force Occupational Safety, Fire and Health Standards, Chapter 14; 29 CFR Part 1910 - Occupational Safety and Health Standards (General Industry Standards) Subpart I; 29 CFR 1910.132; 29 CFR 1910.133; 29 CFR 1910.135; 29 CFR 1910.136; 29 CFR 1910.138
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Train each affected worker on when PPE is necessary, what PPE is necessary, how to properly don, doff, adjust, and wear PPE, the limitations of assigned PPE, and the proper care, maintenance, useful life, and disposal of PPE. Require workers to demonstrate understanding and proper use before performing work requiring PPE, and retrain when workplace conditions, job assignments, PPE types, or worker knowledge gaps make prior training obsolete.
selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Use the work-center JHA, BE occupational health assessment, manufacturer instructions, DAFMAN 91-203 Chapter 14, and local safety office guidance to identify PPE requirements. Supervisors must ensure PPE is provided, used, cleaned, inspected, maintained in sanitary and serviceable condition, and documented in JSTO training records. Cover eye and face protection, head protection, foot protection, hand protection, protective clothing, and respiratory or hearing protection when those programs apply.
selectedModules.notes: Most hazardous noise work areas will have disposable foam plugs hearing protection available to all members if needed.  All members will wear a pair of work gloves anytime they are handling objects with sharp edges or wooded items that can have splinters. Occasionally you may be tasked to move furniture, equipment, or sandbags. You need to wear gloves to prevent cuts and blisters. Gloves may be made of different materials but the palms must be leather. Some shops may also require additional PPE such as eye protection and fall protection harnesses. The supervisor of each functional area is responsible to identify the need, providing the PPE and training as required.

selectedModules.title: Ladder Safety
selectedModules.reference: DAFMAN 91-203 - Air Force Occupational Safety, Fire and Health Standards, Chapter 7
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Train workers to inspect ladders before use, maintain three points of contact, set ladders on stable surfaces, and avoid overreaching or using damaged ladders.
selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Provide hands-on ladder safety training at first assignment, including local storage, damaged-tag procedures, and fall prevention expectations.
selectedModules.notes: Members may need to climb ladders when doing inspections. Ladder training will be a separate entry on the AF Form 55 (or equivalent). Anyone that does self-help projects using ladders at any working height of four feet (4’) must be trained. All training shall include hands-on instruction to include inspection of ladders for defects, possible electrocution hazards, proper positioning, and placement of ladders for various job sites.

selectedModules.title: Forklift / Material Handling Equipment
selectedModules.reference: DAFMAN 91-203 - Air Force Occupational Safety, Fire and Health Standards, Chapter 35; 29 CFR 1910.178 - Powered industrial trucks
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Train powered industrial truck operators in truck-related and workplace-related topics, evaluate performance, and conduct refresher training when unsafe operation, incidents, or workplace changes occur.
selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Use approved lesson plans, hands-on evaluation, and recurring reevaluation before certifying operators. Cover spotter requirements, aircraft proximity rules, and local route restrictions.
selectedModules.notes: As stated in AFI 91-202 members required to utilize powered industrial vehicles in areas of their duties will, IAW DAFMAN 91-203 12.3, be aware of safety hazards associated with operation and complete training to obtain licensing. All qualified operators will carry their issued operator license AF Form 2293 on their person when operating equipment. If a members license has expired they will re-accomplish training prior to vehicle operations.

selectedModules.title: CPR Training
selectedModules.reference: DAFMAN 91-203 - Air Force Occupational Safety, Fire and Health Standards, Chapter 1
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Provide CPR and AED training before assignment where required, and refresh qualification before expiration.
selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Ensure designated responders maintain current certification and understand location and use of local AED assets under the unit mishap prevention program.
selectedModules.notes:
Due to the recent change in DAFMAN 91-203 all unit members required to complete CPR training shall review the following requirements posted October 2021 for changes to policy/requirements.
“1.8. First Aid and Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR) Training. Initial first aid/CPR training shall be accomplished prior to assigning an individual duties where first aid/CPR are requirements of the position. (T-1) All employees requiring CPR training will receive refresher training before current CPR certification expires. (T-1) Unit CPR instructors may be trained by the local Medical Group or trained directly by the American Red Cross or American Heart Association. Unit CPR instructors will, in turn, train unit personnel. (T-1) If CPR training is not provided by the host medical facility, any instructor receiving training directly from the American Red Cross or American Heart Association will be required to maintain the requirements and pay the costs related to maintaining that certification. (T-1) Training will also include Public Access Defibrillator training in accordance with AFI 44-177, Public Access Defibrillator Program. (T-1) Note 1: Self-aid and buddy care may be used to fulfill first aid training requirements; however, it does not cover CPR. Employees performing duties with risk of severe cuts, burns or electrocution, or performing duties in remote locations away from emergency responders will have a plan for immediate medical response pending definitive transfer and care. (T-0) Note 2: Remote location is defined as emergency care that is more than three to four minutes from the workplace.”

selectedModules.title: Government Vehicle / Utility Vehicle Use
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Train vehicle operators on seat belts, speed limits, local traffic hazards, spotter use while backing, and restrictions on electronic device use while driving.
selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Brief operators on unit-specific government vehicle training requirements, local route restrictions, low-speed vehicle rules, and documentation of qualification.
selectedModules.trainingBasis: OSHA 2254 / Vehicle and Mobile Equipment Concepts
selectedModules.notes: IAW DAFI 91-207, 2.2.3. Prior to any unit member being tasked with operating/maintaining Low-Speed Vehicles shall have a current driver’s license, read the operation section of manual, and review training material. Additionally, operators will follow all traffic laws as normal vehicles including posted signs and use directional hand signals when turning. Upon completion of training will be tracked on AF Form 55.

selectedModules.title: Confined Space Program
selectedModules.reference: DAFMAN 91-203 - Air Force Occupational Safety, Fire and Health Standards, Chapter 23; 29 CFR 1910.146 - Permit-required confined spaces
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Train entrants, attendants, supervisors, and rescue personnel so they understand their duties, hazards, signs and symptoms of exposure, communication procedures, and emergency actions before assignment.
selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Provide duty-specific training for permit-required confined space roles, including monitor use, atmospheric hazards, entry permits, and rescue responsibilities before personnel participate in entries.
selectedModules.notes: All members must complete the Confined Spaces CBT
